title: Agentic AI Chat
description: An AI agent embedded in LinkedIn's observability tools, now used by 10,000+ engineers to find an incident's root cause faster.
blurb: Embedded with product engineers, I led end-to-end UX for a conversational AI agent now used across observability tools by 10,000+ LinkedIn engineers. I set the UX principles for LLM interactions, spec'd the conversation, plugin, context, and inline artifact components the team builds on, and designed a custom icon system that signals a trusted, purpose-built tool. The result is faster incident triage and lower cognitive load for engineers in the middle of an incident.

hero.alt: Observe Agent chat home screen, embedded in the observability product
hero.caption: The empty state has three getting-started prompts, not just a blank box waiting for input.

blocks.value: Observe Agent is an AI agent built for LinkedIn's observability tools (alerts, metrics, logs, and deployment history). I led end-to-end UX alongside the product engineers building it: the interaction model, the core components, and the visual identity.
It ships to 10,000+ engineers, who use it to trace incidents like service disruptions and latency spikes to their root cause faster.

sections.heading: What SREs Need Mid-Incident

blocks.value: The users are Site Reliability Engineers and on-call engineers, almost always mid-incident: tabs open across alerting, metrics, logs, and deployment history, under real time pressure. Before designing anything, I wrote down what they needed from the agent, to align the team on the job to be done.

blocks.alt: User-needs statements from a Site Reliability Engineer persona, framed as "I want to…" jobs
blocks.caption: The persona is stated as jobs to be done, not a bio: diagnose, drill into details, revisit later.

sections.heading: The Agent Lives Beside the Data

blocks.value: The agent had to feel native to the product, not bolted onto it. It sits beside the logs and metrics views engineers already use, and acts on them: ask it to show errors during lunch, and it sets the filters in the view itself instead of telling the engineer where to click.

blocks.alt: The agent conversation shown alongside the Logs Explorer, having just applied filters to that view on the engineer's behalf
blocks.caption: The agent doesn't just answer questions: it also takes actions, like applying filters in the Logs Explorer.

sections.heading: A Side Panel, Sized to the Task

blocks.value: I audited how panels already behaved across the product (full-screen views, modals, docked panels) and built a storyboard to argue for a **persistent side panel** that keeps the page in view: narrow for supporting information, wider for create-and-edit, and resizable to whatever balance suits the user.

blocks.alt: Storyboard of side-panel placement options, showing how the chat panel shares screen space with the existing application
blocks.caption: The audit that argued for a resizable side panel instead of a full-screen chat.

sections.heading: An Agent, Not a Chatbot: The Layers Above the Model

blocks.value: Any team can call a foundation LLM; the model was never the design problem. What makes an agent useful mid-incident is everything built on top of it, and I think of Observe Agent as layers:

items: **Context** goes in: the alert, chart, or log an engineer pulls into the conversation.
**Plugins** are the agent's tools, reaching into logs, metrics, alerts, and deployment history.
**Output** comes back as knowledge sources, inline charts, links, and **actions** (like setting Logs Explorer filters) that change the product itself. Actions are where it stops being a chatbot.
**Conversations** span input and output: the evidence the agent reads, and where it reports back.

blocks.alt: Layer diagram of Observe Agent: foundation LLMs at the base, a context layer, plugins bridging into an output layer of sources, inline artifacts, links and CTAs, and actions, with conversations spanning context and output
blocks.caption: The model is the commodity: the domain-specific agent design lives in the layers above it.

sections.heading: Four Components to Help Developers Move Fast

blocks.value: I spec'd the four components everything else builds on: **conversations**; **plugins** for the agent's tools and skills; **context**, such as a chart or a log and the data behind it; and **inline artifacts**, which render answers in place instead of linking out.

blocks.alt: Annotated spec of the conversation component: timestamp, user message, agent message, copy and feedback tools, and chat input
blocks.caption: One conversation pattern, so a thread started in the side panel continues in the full-page view.

blocks.alt: Annotated spec of the plugin flow: hovering the plugin menu button, choosing from the plugin menu, and the chosen plugin added to the chat input as a removable tag
blocks.caption: Picking a plugin points the agent at a specific tool, shown as a tag the engineer can remove.

blocks.alt: Annotated spec of adding context: hovering the intelligence icon on a metric chart card shows "Add to Observe Agent chat," and the chart then appears in the chat input as a removable tag
blocks.caption: Any chart joins the chat with the data behind it, so the engineer doesn't have to describe it.

blocks.alt: Annotated spec of an agent answer with inline artifacts: code snippets, a Metrics Explorer link badge, and an inline metric chart
blocks.caption: The pieces of an answer: code snippets, link badges, and charts, rendered right in the chat.

blocks.alt: Observe Agent in its full-page view, answering with an inline metric chart and a recommendation that links to the Logs Explorer
blocks.caption: All together in the product: the chart answers in place, a Logs Explorer link goes deeper.

sections.heading: An Icon Built to Earn Trust

blocks.value: A generic bot icon would have undercut what this needed most: trust from an engineer deciding whether to act on the agent's answer mid-incident. I audited the sparkle and bot icons other apps use, then designed a mark pairing a sparkle (AI) with a telescope (Observe).

blocks.alt: Icon design work: a comparison audit of sparkle and Slack bot icons, the final telescope-plus-sparkle mark in two variations, and the mark in use in Slack and the web UI
blocks.caption: An audit of AI icons led to a telescope-plus-sparkle mark, validated in Slack and the web UI.

sections.heading: Reflection

blocks.value: The classic UX toolkit didn't disappear here; it changed shape. Personas became jobs to be done, a storyboard audited screen real estate instead of mapping a user flow, and what the team built from wasn't just a wireframe, but also a component spec.

What I'd revisit: the panel model assumes one conversation at a time, untested against an engineer running parallel investigations, which is closer to how a bad incident actually goes. I'd want usage data before deciding whether that calls for side-by-side investigations or just a wider panel.

title: Genomic Data Platform
description: A customer described exactly the comparison tool bioinformaticians needed. It shipped, and became how scientists spot which genes vary across patient cohorts.
blurb: As Senior Staff Interaction Designer, I led UX across Illumina's Connected Analytics platform for multiomic analysis, spanning genomics, proteomics, and spatial transcriptomics apps built on a shared design system, data model, and user base. I grounded the work in evidence-based personas, card sorting with subject matter experts, and ongoing field research, then turned direct customer feedback into shipped visualization features. The result is a cohesive platform that helps scientists compare groups of subjects and accelerate biomarker and drug discovery.
team: UX researchers, bioinformatics subject-matter experts, product stakeholders

hero.alt: The Cohorts survival-comparison view: a Kaplan–Meier curve comparing four subject groups with a p-value confidence matrix
hero.caption: A p-value matrix sits beside the curves: how cohorts diverge, and how confident to be.

blocks.value: Cohorts, by Illumina Connected Analytics, lets customers aggregate and analyze genomic and clinical data using private, public, and partner data sets, then compare groups of subjects to **accelerate biomarker and drug discovery**.

sections.heading: The Research Scientist as the Key Persona

blocks.value: I created **evidence-based personas** from interviews with stakeholders and subject matter experts, and used them to identify user behaviors, tasks, and workflows across three roles: the research scientist, the bioinformatician, and the developer or admin who provisions access. The key persona is the research scientist, whose goal is to discover biomarkers of interest for pharmaceutical or clinical cures.

blocks.alt: Personas for the genomics scientist, bioinformatician, and developer/admin, with goals and a pain-point quote
blocks.caption: Evidence-based personas for three roles, with the research scientist as the key persona.

blocks.value: I ran card sorting sessions with subject matter experts to settle the **shared vocabulary** underneath that persona's work, from genomic sequencing and secondary analysis to case interpretation. Getting that terminology right mattered more than it sounds because it's the language every screen in the platform would eventually use.

blocks.alt: A remote card sorting session grouping genomic analysis terms into workflow phases
blocks.caption: Card sorting with subject matter experts, not a guess: the vocabulary scientists actually use.

sections.heading: Cohorts to Refine, Compare, and Save

blocks.value: I tested low-fidelity prototypes with bioinformaticians who were already using digital workflows to evaluate genetic variants, and their feedback **validated the interaction model**. Giving scientists tools to manage, refine, and analyze cohorts (groups of patients or subjects) helps them get to answers more quickly.

blocks.alt: Low-fidelity cohort-builder prototypes shown to bioinformaticians in interview sessions
blocks.caption: Tested with the bioinformaticians who'd actually run this analysis, not a stand-in audience.

blocks.value: The storyboards worked out the rest of that model before a line of code shipped: **temporary tabs** let a scientist hold several cohorts open to compare side by side, a scatter plot estimates ethnicity against 1000 Genomes Project reference data, cohort size adjusts by filtering out numerical outliers, and a finished cohort can be **saved and shared as a snapshot** rather than rebuilt from scratch by the next person who needs it.

blocks.alt: A storyboard grid walking through building a cohort, comparing multiple cohorts in tabs, estimating ethnicity, and saving a cohort snapshot
blocks.caption: The model in miniature: cohorts you refine, tabs that compare, snapshots you can hand off.

sections.heading: Comparing Multiple Cohorts at Once

blocks.value: I kept synthesizing **customer feedback** from scientists in the field throughout this end-to-end design, and one recorded call reshaped the roadmap. William LaFramboise of Allegheny Health Network described how his team works: compare a breast cancer cohort against colorectal and ovarian cohorts, light up the genes that vary, then drill down into the specific mutations. The takeaway was bigger than any one chart: scientists need to **compare multiple cohorts at a time**.

blocks.alt: A recorded customer call with William LaFramboise of Allegheny Health Network describing the need to compare gene variance across cohorts
blocks.caption: A real customer call: compare breast, colorectal, and ovarian cancer cohorts side by side.

blocks.value: The **Comparisons** view shipped in response. A scientist opens up to four cohorts together, sees their demographics charted side by side, and runs the same analyses across all of them: attributes, correlation, marker frequency, genes, and survival. **Marker Frequency**, shown here, lights up the up- and down-regulated genes across lung, prostate, uterine, and breast cohorts at once.

blocks.alt: The Marker Frequency comparison view: up- and down-regulated gene percentages across four named cohorts at once
blocks.caption: Four cohorts in one comparison, with Marker Frequency as one of six analyses.

blocks.value: From there, the **Genes** tab in the single cohort view supports the drill-down LaFramboise described: mutation types color-coded by gene, so a scientist can spot common mutations before digging into specific variants.

blocks.alt: The Genes tab: a mutation-type heat map by gene, color-coded by variant class, for the active cohort
blocks.caption: Mutation types by gene, color-coded by variant class, for a single cohort.

sections.heading: What User Testing Changed

blocks.value: User testing kept finding the smaller misses that research alone doesn't catch. Mid-session, a participant hit a real problem: rare variants were all squished to the bottom of the plot, impossible to tell apart. The fix that shipped was a single **Invert Y-axis** toggle, so rare variants aren't lost at the bottom of their own chart.

blocks.alt: A user-testing session where a participant asks to invert the y-axis so rare variants are visible
blocks.caption: “The rare variants are squished to the bottom.” The fix: an Invert Y-axis toggle.

blocks.value: The same testing surfaced an **unmet need**: scientists wanted to see the distribution of variant types per gene. Radar charts gave each gene its own shape across six structural variant types, comparable at a glance down an entire results page.

blocks.alt: A grid of radar charts showing structural-variant type distribution per gene
blocks.caption: Six structural variant types per gene, one shape each, comparable at a glance.

blocks.value: Testing also showed what came next. Once a scientist spotted a gene of interest in the radar charts, they wanted to **drill into that one gene** and see how its alterations were distributed across disease subtypes. The Molecular Breakdown view answers that with a grouped bar chart: one gene, five alteration types, broken down by a subject attribute such as disease, with a toggle to stack the bars.

blocks.alt: The Molecular Breakdown view: a grouped bar chart of PCLAF alterations by variant type across ten cancer types, with a Stacked/Grouped toggle
blocks.caption: Drilling into one gene: PCLAF alterations across ten cancer types, grouped or stacked.

sections.heading: One System Across Three Different Data Types

blocks.value: Cohorts wasn't the only app I owned. I applied the same visual language and component system to **Connected Multiomics**, Illumina's proteomics and spatial transcriptomics apps, so the platform reads as one product. The science differs, but all three visualize gene or protein expression: the proteomics volcano plot could have served Cohorts too, but never made the roadmap.

blocks.alt: The Connected Multiomics proteomics viewer with a volcano plot and per-protein box plots
blocks.caption: Different science, same system: new chart types, same chart-beside-data-table pattern.

blocks.alt: The Connected Multiomics spatial viewer showing a tissue slice with a UMAP and transcript counts
blocks.caption: Spatial transcriptomics pushes hardest: a tissue slice and a UMAP plot, same components.

sections.heading: Reflection

blocks.value: The analysis tools were only half the product. Scientists mostly compare affected samples against unaffected ones, so a comparison is only as good as the cohorts on both sides of it, and finding a matched healthy cohort was often the hardest part. That's the pain point behind the key persona's struggle to find enough data, and why offering both disease and healthy data sets mattered. Shriners, one of our heaviest users, brought their own scoliosis data sets and compared them against healthy data sets in the platform.

I proposed going further with a **data marketplace**, where research labs could share data sets with one another, so one lab's data could become another lab's comparison cohort. It was a good idea that never became a prioritized backlog item. If I revisited it, I'd make the case in product-value terms: every data set added to the platform means more comparisons scientists can run, and more reason for labs to keep their research there.

title: AI Recommendations
description: An inline recommendation model for Informatica's data-integration products, plus a precision-tracking method I convinced cross-functional teams to ship so the model keeps learning from what developers actually choose.
blurb: As Principal UX Designer, I brought AI-predicted best practices into Informatica's data integration products, designing an inline recommendation model that suggests the next set of transformations without breaking the developer's flow. I partnered with ML engineers to shape the interaction model across cloud and desktop, and designed a lightweight precision tracking method that I convinced cross-functional teams to ship, so the model retrains on real user choices.
team: Machine learning engineers, UX researchers, UX partners, executive leadership

hero.alt: The mapping designer with the recommendations panel alongside the canvas: each suggestion explained with a Show Me link, two marked applied, and a lightbulb on a link in the canvas
hero.caption: Each recommendation explains itself, and developers apply it without leaving the mapping.

blocks.value: As **Principal User Experience Designer** at Informatica, I designed an AI feature that predicts and suggests the next data transformation a developer needs, trained on anonymized mapping patterns across customer tenants. I partnered with machine learning engineers and UX researchers to shape the interaction model across both the desktop client and the newer cloud product.

The recommendations only work if developers trust them and don't have to leave their flow to use them. That meant designing them to appear inline in the canvas first, with a side panel alongside for the explanation and history the canvas had no room for, and building a way to prove the model was actually getting better instead of just declaring it was.

sections.heading: How the Model Learns What to Recommend

blocks.value: A mapping is a data transformation workflow that moves data from a source to a target through a sequence of user-specified transformations. The model analyzes matching sequences across anonymized mappings from multiple customer tenants and, based on prior usage patterns, **predicts the “next set”** of transformations a developer is likely to add. Developers built mappings in two designers, the desktop client and the newer cloud product, so the recommendations had to fit one mental model across both.

blocks.alt: The mapping designer shown in both the desktop client and the cloud product
blocks.caption: Desktop and cloud mapping designers: different products, one mental model for developers.

sections.heading: Two Personas, One Canvas

blocks.value: My user research pointed to the **Data Integration Developer** as the primary persona. Gartner's research introduced a second: the **Citizen Developer**, a non-technical subject-matter expert who needs to build integrations without writing code. Both had to work in the same mapping canvas, part of why the recommendations couldn't afford to ask either of them to learn something new.

blocks.alt: The two target personas, the Data Integration Developer and the non-technical Citizen Developer, from Gartner research, beside an illustration of the mapping designer and its field mapping
blocks.caption: Two personas, one canvas: the Data Integration Developer and the non-technical Citizen Developer.

sections.heading: Inline in the Canvas: Ghost Shape or Menu

blocks.value: I advocated for surfacing recommendations in the canvas first, right where the developer is already working. The comparison I used was predictive text: the suggestion shows up where you're typing, not somewhere else on the screen.

blocks.alt: A messaging app suggesting the next words inline, used as an analogy for recommendations that appear where the developer is working
blocks.caption: Like predictive text, the suggestion appears right where you're already working.

blocks.value: Inline still left the interaction model open, so I explored several. The most literal was a “ghost shape”: the recommended step drawn with a dashed outline right where it would go, accepted or dismissed in place. The one we chose was a menu: a lightbulb appears in the canvas automatically, prompting the developer to open a list of transformations with the recommended ones at the top. The menu won because it offered more. Developers still had every standard transformation below the recommendations, not just the ones the model surfaced.

blocks.alt: Concept renderings of recommendation interaction models in the mapping canvas: dashed ghost shapes with accept and dismiss buttons, a stacked set of options, and a transformation menu with recommended items at the top
blocks.caption: Higher-fidelity explorations: ghost shapes, stacked options, and the menu we chose.

blocks.alt: The transformation menu with AI-recommended options marked by a distinct lightbulb icon
blocks.caption: The menu: recommended transformations at the top, every standard one still below.

blocks.value: I specified every state engineering needed: with and without a recommendation, on a link or a standalone shape, default and hover, and spacing when several links leave one shape.

blocks.alt: An annotated interaction spec comparing link and shape states with and without a recommendation: no button by default, a menu button on hover, an orange lightbulb when a recommendation exists that turns into the menu button on hover, and spacing for multiple links from a router
blocks.caption: The spec for every state: when the lightbulb shows, when it becomes a menu, and where.

blocks.value: Inline shipped first, on my recommendation. A side panel followed, and it earned its place by doing what the canvas had no room for: explaining why each recommendation was shown, which is what made it credible; a **“Show Me”** action that took the developer straight to the configuration being recommended; and a running record of what had already been applied.

sections.heading: From Napkin Sketch to Shipped Interaction

blocks.value: The same exploration started on paper, at lower fidelity: the ghost shape, the menu, and a few variations on each. A storyboard worked out how the side panel and the in-canvas cues fit together: new recommendations appear automatically in the panel as cards, each with a “Show Me” action that jumps to the recommendation in context; lightbulbs mark recommended values in place, with the explanation in a tooltip; and dismissed recommendations stay reachable under their own tab instead of disappearing for good.

blocks.alt: Hand sketches of recommendation interactions in the mapping canvas: a dashed ghost shape between source and target, a menu of recommended Lookups opened from a button on a link, a stacked set of options, and several button styles
blocks.caption: The same exploration in sketch form: ghost shapes, a menu, and stacked options.

blocks.alt: An eight-frame storyboard walking through when recommendations surface, how they are explained, and how they are accepted, dismissed, or recovered
blocks.caption: The storyboard worked out how the side panel and the in-canvas cues fit together.

blocks.alt: An animated prototype showing a recommendation appearing and being accepted in the mapping canvas
blocks.caption: An animated prototype carried the interaction to engineering before any of it was built.

blocks.alt: Visual explorations applying Informatica's CLAIRE AI branding to the recommendations panel
blocks.caption: CLAIRE, Informatica's AI brand, applied to the shipped panel: the swirl mark and lightbulb icon.

sections.heading: Teaching the Feature Where It Lives

blocks.value: Introducing the feature followed the same rule as the feature itself: put it where developers already work. Instead of pointing developers to release notes, I designed an in-app “What's New” message that appeared inside the mapping designer: a short looping animation of a transformation being added right on the canvas, with the recommended ones at the top of the menu. In the first week after release, 1,145 developers saw it, and 85% of views ended in a click on one of its buttons.

blocks.alt: An in-app What's New message titled Add transformations directly on the mapping canvas, animating a hover on a link that opens the transformation menu with recommended options at the top, then adds a recommended Lookup between source and target
blocks.caption: An in-app “What's New” loop showed the feature in the canvas, where developers would use it.

blocks.value: In customer interviews after release, one developer put it plainly: “Since the last upgrade they added this function that's pretty cool.” (Keri-Ann Bowen, ETL Developer, University of Maryland)

sections.heading: Influencing the Team to Prioritize a Precision Method

blocks.value: A recommendation is only worth showing if it's actually right, so I designed a simple method to measure that: track what the model predicted against what the developer actually picked, a true positive if they match, a false positive if they don't. The machine learning engineers saw the value right away. My part was proactively influencing the team to make building the instrumentation a high priority. Once it shipped, false positives fed back into the model so it adjusted toward what developers were actually choosing.

blocks.alt: A diagram contrasting a true-positive and a false-positive prediction, feeding user selections back to improve the model
blocks.caption: The precision method I designed: a match is a true positive, a miss retrains the model.

sections.heading: Convincing Leadership to Modernize the Whole Product

blocks.value: The recommendations panel highlighted how dated the rest of the product's visual design had gotten by comparison. I worked with UX partners to redesign the look and feel, then made the case to executive leadership that modernizing the UI was worth the investment on its own, not just as a backdrop for the AI feature.

blocks.alt: The modernized visual design language applied to the mapping designer
blocks.caption: The modernized visual language I argued for: worth shipping on its own, not just a backdrop.

sections.heading: Reflection

blocks.value: The classic toolkit didn't disappear on this project, it just carried different weight. The sketches and storyboard weren't there to document a process, they settled a real interaction question (where does a prediction live, and what happens when it's wrong) before any model output existed to design around. The artifact that reached furthest beyond the design team was the true-positive/false-positive diagram: it doubled as a spec and as the case for building the tracking early.

What I'd revisit: the model treated every mismatch as its own mistake. But a developer can pass over a good recommendation for reasons that have nothing to do with it, like habit or a team convention, and the model still learns from that choice. I'd want a way to tell a wrong recommendation apart from a right one that simply wasn't picked, so the model retrains toward best practices, not just habits.

title: Operational Insights
description: A new monitoring product built for the Monday-morning check: big numbers at a glance, deeper analysis one click down. It shipped, and customers said it had "the right kinds of metrics."
blurb: A data monitoring dashboard built for the quick daily glance: big actionable numbers first, deep analysis one click away. Shipped, with customers calling out "the right kinds of metrics."

hero.alt: The Operational Insights overview dashboard: job-status fast facts above the two key metrics, top secure agents, and a data-volume heat map
hero.caption: The Monday-morning check: fast facts first, then key metrics, with detail views a click away.

blocks.value: As **Principal User Experience Designer** at Informatica, I designed a new product for monitoring data-integration operations. A UX researcher and I interviewed and observed users as they walked us through their workflows. One key finding: small teams, typically five or fewer developers and one manager, both build data-integration jobs and monitor the daily flow of data. I designed the overview dashboard to give those teams a quick look at their operations, what I called the **"Monday‑morning check."**

sections.heading: Big Numbers, Not Pie Charts

blocks.value: Observing users made one thing clear: the first look is about **large, actionable numbers**, or "fast facts," not the pie and donut charts common to most dashboards. I built the fast-facts row around that finding.

blocks.alt: Hand sketches labeled Fast Facts and Insights, next to three higher-fidelity mockups of the job-status fast facts, two with insight or alert cards beside them
blocks.caption: Turning what users told us into fast facts and insight cards, from sketches to mockups.

blocks.value: The fast-facts concept carried through several rounds of higher-fidelity mockups into what shipped. The insight cards beside it, alerts for jobs that ran longer or processed fewer rows than usual, were well received by product management but didn't make it to the top of the roadmap.
The interviews also surfaced two **key metrics**: Rows Processed and Number of Jobs. Each shows its total beside a miniature chart, and hovering over a column reveals the detail behind it.

blocks.alt: Rows Processed and Number of Jobs shown as a large value beside a small bar chart, with a hover tooltip breaking a bar into succeeded, warning, and failed counts
blocks.caption: Two key metrics: Number of Jobs stacks its columns to break each count down by status.

sections.heading: Every Fast Fact Is a Doorway

blocks.value: Every fast fact needed a next step. From a single number, a user drops into **detail views**, such as a filtered list of failed jobs or scheduled tasks by runtime environment, without losing the thread back to where they started.

blocks.alt: The job-status fast-facts row with arrows connecting the Failed and Scheduled tiles to a filtered job list and a scheduled-tasks chart
blocks.caption: From a number to the analysis behind it, such as the Failed and Scheduled detail views.

sections.heading: Time Series for the Second Glance

blocks.value: The second glance goes deeper. **Time-series charts** of the two key metrics, lines for Rows Processed and stacked columns for Number of Jobs, correlate both against the projects and folders they belong to, over whatever date range the user picks.

blocks.alt: An analysis screen with a multi-series line chart of rows processed by project above a stacked-column chart of job counts over a week
blocks.caption: Not every question fits a single number: detail views chart the key metrics by project.

sections.heading: Customers Were Already Building This by Hand

blocks.value: Customer interviews revealed that teams were **piecing together their own monitoring** using emailed reports, ad-hoc dashboards, and a Slack channel where their tools posted job updates all day. Those workarounds generated ideas for visualization and reporting features, and one bigger idea.

blocks.alt: A collage of customer-built monitoring: ad-hoc dashboards, an email summary of processed-rows statistics, and an automated Slack channel of task-flow updates
blocks.caption: What customers built for themselves first: emailed reports, dashboards, a Slack status channel.

sections.heading: Bringing the Fast Facts Into Slack

blocks.value: Customers already had a Slack channel they checked all day, so instead of asking them to open another dashboard, I proposed bringing the same fast facts and anomaly alerts there. I took the idea to product management and designed a prototype: a bot that posted alerts straight into the channel and performed actions on request, such as restarting a stuck agent or explaining an anomaly, right where the team was already talking. It demoed well. It did not make the next roadmap.

blocks.alt: A Slack conversation in the Data Integration channel: teammates asking the CLAIRE bot about anomalies and to restart a stuck agent, with the bot posting a rows-processed chart in response
blocks.caption: CLAIRE, a Slack bot prototype that brings alerts and answers to where the team already talks.

sections.heading: Connector Names Over Company Logos

blocks.value: An early mockup put company logos, such as Salesforce, AWS, Oracle, and Workday, on the Top Targets and Top Sources bar charts in place of plain text labels. It was a popular idea with product marketers, but it wouldn't scale well because Informatica supports hundreds of connector types and custom connections never come with a logo. The shipped product labels each connector by name instead, a design that works for every connector, custom ones included.

blocks.alt: An early dashboard mockup with company logos, such as Salesforce, AWS, Oracle, and Workday, in place of connector names on the Top Targets and Top Sources bar charts
blocks.caption: An early mockup where I tried company logos in place of connector names in the charts.

sections.heading: Blue for Real, Green for Predicted

blocks.value: I determined that predictive features needed visual cues to keep actual values from blurring together with the forecast. A semantic **color code** did it: blue for what happened, green for what the model predicts. I added a "How was this prediction made?" link beside it, so developers could question the forecast, not just trust it.

blocks.alt: A rows-processed line chart in blue above a green shaded area chart labeled Projected Rows Processed, powered by CLAIRE, with a pointer on the How was this prediction made? link
blocks.caption: Blue for what happened, green for the model's prediction, plus a way to ask how it was made.

sections.heading: What Shipped, and What Users Said

blocks.value: After launch, I spoke with customers to learn whether the design was meeting their needs. The best reaction came on a call with Nick Marty, an Informatica user, with the live dashboard shared on screen: **"I really like Operational Insights. It's got the right kinds of metrics."**

blocks.alt: A video call with the shipped Operational Insights dashboard on an Informatica user's screen, next to the quote: I really like Operational Insights. It's got the right kinds of metrics.
blocks.caption: The shipped product on a user's own screen: fast facts first, connectors labeled by name.

sections.heading: Reflection

blocks.value: Talking with Informatica customers sparked more ideas than one release could hold. Part of my role was to explore the strongest ones early and give product management real options, knowing the roadmap would decide which shipped first.

Of those, the Slack bot is the one I would push to production first. Customers had already proven the concept by building rougher versions of it themselves. With today's LLMs, it would be even more powerful.

Trust in the AI prediction mattered as much as reading it correctly. The "How was this prediction made?" link was our answer, but the prediction UI hadn't shipped while I was there, so I never saw whether it changed how much teams trusted the forecast. That is the open question I would go back and answer.

title: Developer Experience
description: A developer portal built from scratch for GE's Predix cloud, where I led design and product management: an MVP catalog shipped fast, went in front of Gartner, and launched in full.
blurb: A developer portal and admin console built from scratch for GE's Predix cloud, where I led design and product management. The MVP catalog shipped fast, got demoed to Gartner, and launched in full.
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer and acting Technical Product Manager, GE Digital
team: Agile product team of developers and designers

hero.alt: The Predix Developer Network home page: an "Industrial IoT Platform" hero above a "How Predix Works" diagram
hero.caption: Show, don't tell: an app to try, a tutorial to learn from, and a showcase app built on the platform.

blocks.value: I led design and product management for a new web portal and administration console for an industrial cloud platform, **built from scratch with an agile team**. The design goal was to get a software developer from a first visit to a running application as quickly as possible. I later deployed a base app live on stage in under five minutes.

sections.heading: A Persona to Test Ideas Against

blocks.value: The work centered on one primary user, **Elaine the Software Architect**, and the decisions she makes along her journey. Casting her as the main character in storyboards let the team generate ideas quickly and validate each one against what she actually needed.

blocks.alt: A storyboard panel of Elaine browsing the Predix catalog and trying an interactive API test console against a live wind turbine
blocks.caption: “Listing APIs is nice, but I want to try the technology.” Elaine's line drove the API test console.

sections.heading: Storyboards to Find the Critical Features

blocks.value: Product storyboards walked the full path (sign up, build, deploy, monitor) and surfaced the features that actually mattered. The target was **a base application up and running in under five minutes**, and I tested it in person with developers.

blocks.alt: A storyboard showing Elaine's app auto-deploying to the cloud and an application dashboard where she reviews usage stats
blocks.caption: Elaine's app is running in under five minutes (panel 13), the target the whole flow was built around.

sections.heading: Lo-Fi Wireframes and Motion Prototypes

blocks.value: Before anything was built, low-fidelity wireframes drove early iteration on the catalog and console layouts, and **After Effects motion prototypes** tested how the interactions should behave.

blocks.alt: Wireframes of the Predix catalog of starter packs and services beside a console showing alerts, resource usage, and favorite apps
blocks.caption: The catalog wireframe led with runnable starter packs, not just a service directory to browse.

blocks.alt: A silent motion study testing hover and active-item transitions in the Predix docs navigation
blocks.caption: This behavior was proven in motion before a single line of production code existed.

sections.heading: From Beta to General Release

blocks.value: The beta put the catalog and the console in developers' hands as soon as possible, so we could rapidly gather feedback. At the same time, I led the UX design team in a collaborative effort with product marketing to rebrand the platform, closely followed by a visual redesign.

blocks.alt: The Predix beta console's app view: configuration, running status, and a recent events list for a seed app
blocks.caption: In beta, one screen showed an app's configuration, live status, and recent events.

blocks.value: We shipped an **MVP catalog of cloud services** and demoed it to analysts, including Gartner, months ahead of the full launch.

blocks.alt: The launched Predix catalog page, organized into Services, Analytics, and Apps tabs
blocks.caption: The launched catalog, after the rebrand and visual redesign that followed the beta release.

sections.heading: Driving Developer Adoption

blocks.value: A good UI wasn't going to be enough on its own. I pitched the marketing team on funding a series of **coding videos** aimed at developers, not a generic product reel, and won the budget. The videos lived on the community site, next to the developer forum and blog.

blocks.alt: The Predix community page with forum and blog links and an embedded "A Developer's Take on Predix" video
blocks.caption: “Hear what a Predix developer has to say”: developers talking to developers, not a product pitch.

blocks.value: I put together a quick storyboard to guide the shoot, then directed the lean crew that shot the videos.

blocks.alt: A storyboard for the developer video series: title card, medium close with lower thirds, over-the-shoulder, and screen capture shots
blocks.caption: The storyboard favored over-the-shoulder and screen capture: show the code, not talk about it.

sections.heading: Taking the Product to Customers

blocks.value: After launch, I represented the product at GE's Minds + Machines and Industrial Internet events, carrying customer needs straight back into the roadmap. At one of them, Industrial Internet for Developers, I deployed an app live on stage in under five minutes.

blocks.alt: Jim Reed in conversation with a customer on the show floor at GE's Minds + Machines conference
blocks.caption: On the Minds + Machines show floor, hearing firsthand what customers needed next.

sections.heading: Reflection

blocks.value: This product taught me a lot, including how to lead a team of designers and developers. Taking on the PM role gave me empathy for product managers: it's a challenge to choose 10 features from a list of 100 when the team only has capacity for 10. The feedback from the team was very positive, and I think being a designer and storyteller helped me define features clearly for the team to build.

title: Additive Manufacturing
description: A monitoring dashboard that turns each 3D printer's sensor data into one Availability Score. Once it shipped, users read the first release's donut charts as print progress, not availability, so I replaced them with a number, a color, and a day-over-day trend arrow.
blurb: A monitoring dashboard that gives additive manufacturing teams a clear Availability Score for every 3D printer and across the whole fleet.
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer, GE Digital
team: Another visual designer, with user discovery done alongside the lead engineer and architect

hero.alt: The Additive Console's fleet-wide Availability view: an aggregate 58% score with nine ranked facility cards below it
hero.caption: One Availability Score for the whole fleet, with every facility's own score ranked below.

blocks.value: GE Additive's customers run fleets of industrial metal 3D printers, and the business goal behind this product was simple: keep every printer **printing for as much of its available time as possible**. As Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer at GE Digital, I designed the **Additive Console**, a monitoring dashboard built around that goal. It gathers each printer's sensor data into one number, an **Availability Score**, calculated per machine and rolled up per facility and across the whole fleet.

sections.heading: Why the Donut Chart Had to Go

blocks.value: The business goal picked the score: of the three factors in Overall Equipment Effectiveness (availability, performance, and quality), availability measures how much of the time a printer is actually printing. The first release showed it as a **donut chart**, matching the dashboard's visual language, but that's also the ring the printers use on their touchscreens for build progress, so the score read as progress, not availability.

blocks.alt: The Additive Console's overview, a grid of OEE donut charts per facility, with a printer's own progress donut overlaid in the corner
blocks.caption: Users found the clash: facility scores used the same ring printers show for build progress.

blocks.value: Feedback from users of the shipped dashboard surfaced the mix-up directly, and the next release's fix was blunt: drop the ring for **a number, a color indicator, and an arrow for the day-over-day trend**, none of which the printers' touchscreens use.

blocks.alt: Side-by-side options labeled "donut" and "not donut": a circular gauge versus a large percentage with an up arrow and a color bar
blocks.caption: The redesigned solution, at right: a number, color bar, and trend arrow that can't be read as progress.

sections.heading: An MVP in One Sprint, Then Built for Additive

blocks.value: Before any of that, the dashboard started from an MVP, not a blank page. Each printer already streamed its sensor data through a Predix Edge device, and in one sprint the team and I turned it into a card per machine, using existing UI patterns for monitoring Industrial Internet edge devices. Every value was there, but nothing answered a manager's real question: **"How are my printers doing?"** The next step was refining it for the additive use case.

blocks.alt: The MVP dashboard: stacked per-machine summary cards, each with job progress, a 30-day utilization bar chart, and raw sensor tag values
blocks.caption: Before learning from users, a one-sprint MVP showed the data, not yet the value in it.

sections.heading: Watching Builds Get Tracked by Hand

blocks.value: To refine the MVP for how additive teams actually work, I did **contextual research at the Additive Technology Center (ATC) in West Chester, Ohio**. I observed the manufacturing process and interviewed operators, process engineers, and reliability engineers at their machines, not in a conference room. Builds were still tracked by hand on whiteboards. The dashboard needed to make build status live and shared, so no one had to walk the floor to read it.

blocks.alt: Site-visit photos of engineers reviewing a hand-written production whiteboard, standing at a control center, and operating a metal 3D printer
blocks.caption: During my observation, I discovered build status was tracked by hand on shop-floor whiteboards.

blocks.alt: A selfie at the facility, wearing safety glasses in front of a jet engine on display
blocks.caption: Contextual research meant safety glasses and a jet engine, not just a conference room.

sections.heading: A Journey Map and Personas Before Any Sketches

blocks.value: That research shaped three artifacts. A journey map identified **two MVP opportunities**: availability dashboards for managers and mobile build status for operators. Three personas made those users concrete. Only then did I sketch, starting from a persona's view.

blocks.alt: A journey map with a top row of part-manufacturing steps and a lower band of horizontal functions, each tied to a role
blocks.caption: The journey map flagged two MVP opportunities: dashboards for managers, mobile for operators.

blocks.alt: Three persona cards: Charlize, Fleet Manager; Joy, Process Engineer; and Stacey, Operator, each with a time horizon, a quote, a goal, and a challenge
blocks.caption: Three personas, three time horizons: from a year of fleet trends down to a single build.

blocks.alt: A hand-drawn sketch of a browser dashboard showing per-machine availability percentages, beside a smiling user
blocks.caption: Sketching for a persona: a human in the frame kept the team focused on customer value.

sections.heading: One Score, From the Fleet Down to One Job

blocks.value: The fleet view at the top of this page was the entry point. Clicking a facility drilled down to a Builds table of every machine's current job; clicking a machine drilled down again, to one job's Availability and progress, tracked against time elapsed and remaining. One score, followed from the whole fleet down to **one job on one printer**: the clear read the MVP's per-machine cards had been missing.

blocks.alt: The Additive Console's Builds table for one facility: every machine's job at that site, with status and progress bars
blocks.caption: One facility: every machine's current build, sorted by status and start time.

blocks.alt: A drill-down to one machine's current print job, CL-3031, with an Availability ring, a progress bar, and a job list
blocks.caption: An early-round mockup, before the redesign: one machine's current job, with its Availability ring.

sections.heading: Mobile for On-Call Operators

blocks.value: In user interviews, operators said they wanted to **monitor builds from home** and come in only if a build stopped. My early sketch, hand-drawn green and red bars on a phone, carried into the mockup almost as drawn: a **Builds** list, color-coded by status.

blocks.alt: Side by side: a hand holding a phone with a sketch-style "My Machines" list with green and red progress bars, and a phone mockup of a color-coded Builds list
blocks.caption: Off shift, an operator can check every build's state on a phone, green and red at a glance.

sections.heading: Reflection

blocks.value: The donut chart wasn't a bad guess. It matched the rest of the dashboard's visual system, and that's exactly why it was risky: a data visualization component that looks right in a style guide can still fail next to the one screen operators already trust for another metric. Customers caught it after launch, but it's worth asking whether checking it against the printer's own UI earlier, before the first mockup, would have caught it before it shipped.

Then again, that's what shipping early is for. Putting out an MVP in one sprint, then shipping each round and listening to the people using it, meant the team learned from working software instead of debating mockups, and could adjust quickly. Get something real in front of users, learn, adjust: that loop is what turns each round into more customer value.

title: Machine Learning for Operators
description: A guided model-training wizard, shipped inside GE's Predix-powered AI Workbench, that let operations engineers, not data scientists, build the machine-learning models behind a plant's production forecasts.
blurb: Design that put machine learning model training in the hands of the operations engineers who know the equipment best, no data scientist required.
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer, GE Digital
team: Product managers and international scrum teams across California, Bangalore, and New York; UX researchers

hero.alt: An Operations Optimization dashboard with a Capacity Advisor recommendation and Digital Twin vs. actual output trends for three gas turbines
hero.caption: The optimizer quantifies its own trade directly: -100 MWh banked against +10 MW gained at peak.

blocks.value: Training an accurate machine-learning model normally takes a data scientist. The **operations engineers closest to industrial sensor data don't have that background**, but they understand the equipment better than anyone. I designed a guided model-training tool that put that work directly in their hands.

sections.heading: Bidding Into the Market, One Percent at a Time

blocks.value: The stakes were concrete, not abstract. A power plant manager bids into the electricity market based on how much power the plant will produce. **Underproduce and the plant eats a regulatory penalty. Overproduce and it burns fuel that never becomes revenue.** A model good enough to trust was the difference between a bid that held and one that didn't.

blocks.alt: A case study slide over a photo of a power plant control room: a power plant manager needs to predict output accurately enough to bid into the electricity market
blocks.caption: Underproduce and pay a regulatory penalty. Overproduce and waste fuel that's not earning revenue.

sections.heading: On-Site Visits to Watch the Real Workflow

blocks.value: With a UX researcher, I visited customer sites to watch **Reliability Engineers, Data Analysts, and Data Scientists** work the floor, then ran follow-up sessions sketching the model-building flow with them directly.

blocks.alt: A collage of site-visit photos: engineers at multi-monitor stations, a whiteboard control center, and participants sketching data curves by hand
blocks.caption: Reliability engineers sketched their own data curves before I ever showed them a wireframe.

sections.heading: Let Them See the Data Before They Trust the Model

blocks.value: Interviews kept returning to one thing: **before anyone would trust a trained model, they wanted to see the data it was trained on.** I designed the data library so every field shows its own distribution, range, and outlier count up front, and added a correlation view so a hunch about two signals could be checked before committing to a technique.

blocks.alt: The AI Workbench data library: a field summary table for four sensor fields above a time-series chart of wind speed and acceleration
blocks.caption: Every field gets its own distribution, range, and outlier count before training starts.

blocks.alt: A correlation coefficient matrix across nine sensor fields beside a correlation density heat map of torque against kWh
blocks.caption: Before training a model, an engineer could check whether two signals actually correlate.

sections.heading: A Wizard That Trades Flexibility for Guardrails

blocks.value: I broke the data-science process into a **fixed five-step wizard** (Add Data, Prepare, Select Technique, Select Features, Train & Test) instead of leaving it open-ended. The trade was deliberate: less flexibility than a notebook, but a path an operations engineer could actually finish. A trained model doesn't just sit with the person who built it, either. Publishing it to a shared Analytics Catalog makes it available to the next team that needs the same kind of model.

blocks.alt: The Train Machine Learning Model screen: a five-step stepper, training configuration on the left, and an accuracy donut with an ROC curve on the right
blocks.caption: Five fixed steps end in one choice: test the model, deploy it, or publish it as a template.

blocks.alt: A conceptual map of Data Engineer, Data Scientist, and Analytic Developer roles moving data and trained models through a Data Catalog, Model Builder, and Analytics Catalog
blocks.caption: Publishing to the Analytics Catalog turned one team's trained model into shared infrastructure.

sections.heading: Prognostic Equipment Dashboards

blocks.value: Model output feeds **prognostic dashboards** built for low-light industrial control rooms: a dark UI comparing the Digital Twin's expected output against actual readings, with a capacity optimizer recommending action, like the peak-fire call shown at the top of this page.

sections.heading: Monitoring for Data Drift

blocks.value: The data-science process doesn't end at deployment, it's iterative and perpetual because of **data drift**. Monitoring tools plot predicted against actual values and mark retraining events, so an operator sees when accuracy slips before it becomes a bigger problem.

blocks.alt: Power-output and heat-rate charts for a gas turbine overlaying actual and predicted lines, with diamond markers on retraining events
blocks.caption: Each diamond marks a retraining event, so drift is a visible line, not a support ticket.

sections.heading: Reflection

blocks.value: The classic UX toolkit didn't disappear here, it just moved earlier and got more literal: the closest thing to a storyboard was an engineer sketching a data curve on a legal pad while explaining drift to me directly. Two things I'd revisit. The accuracy donut collapses a model's fit to one number; it reads at a glance, but I never tested whether an operations engineer without a statistics background reads '69.91%' as roughly right or as a rounding error away from wrong, and the honest caveats (test-set size, feature confidence) run deeper than one number can carry. And the correlation matrix, while inviting, assumes the viewer already knows what a correlation coefficient is. I put it in front of reliability engineers on faith that a color-coded grid would teach itself; I'd want real data on whether it did.

title: Mobile Emergency System
description: A next-generation 911 app that kept a genuinely complex, multi-party emergency system simple under stress. It shipped across iOS, Android, and desktop, giving operators, responders, and citizens one shared, real-time picture of an incident.
blurb: A Next Generation 911 app where operators, responders, and citizens share location, photos, and video in real time, designed to stay usable under stress. Shipped across iOS, Android, and desktop.
team: User experience designers and developers for iOS, Android, backend, and web UI

hero.alt: Three iPhone screens of the AtHoc app: a message list, an emergency report with a photo and map, and a map of alert zones
hero.caption: Three screens, one system: the message feed, an emergency report, and the live map.

blocks.value: As **Principal Product Designer** at BlackBerry AtHoc, I designed a next-generation 911 service that let dispatchers, emergency operators, responders, and citizens share critical information (text, geolocation, photos, video) during an incident, across **iOS, Android, and desktop**. Every screen was built around one goal: make a genuinely complex, multi-party system feel simple to use under stress.

sections.heading: Emergency Controls Borrowed From the Hardware on the Wall

blocks.value: Under stress, people fall back on instinct, not instructions. I grounded the app's visual language in the **physical hardware people already trust in an emergency**: call boxes, pull stations, strobes, the red SOS button on the wall. That reference, not a generic style guide, is why the app's emergency control is a saturated red circle instead of a flat UI accent color.

blocks.alt: A mood board of emergency hardware photos: SOS buttons, fire pull stations, call boxes, and red strobe lights
blocks.caption: A wall-mounted alarm reads instantly. The app's emergency button borrows that same instant read.

sections.heading: Ten Screen Templates, Then Every Path Between Them

blocks.value: Fast, rough sketches identified **ten screen templates** the app would need, menu, splash screen, registration, default list, slider, emergency composer, message, reply, report list, and send report, before any layout work began.

blocks.alt: A grid of hand sketches labeled menu, splash, register, default, slider, emergency, message, reply, report list, and send report
blocks.caption: Ten templates settled here, menu to send report, before any screen was actually laid out.

blocks.value: **Screen-flow diagrams** then mapped every user action in the app: duress, check in, report, tracking, and inbox, including the branches only an operator could take and the paths that succeeded with or without attached media.

blocks.alt: A branching flow diagram of numbered app screens covering duress, check-in, report, tracking, and inbox use cases
blocks.caption: Every path branches: operator-only screens split off, and reports succeed with or without media.

blocks.value: Low-fidelity wireframes carried that flow into actual **layout and annotation** for the send-emergency-message screen specifically: the always-visible emergency call button, the message and media-attachment controls, inline location, and the thread of operator alerts and citizen replies.

blocks.alt: Annotated wireframes of a send-emergency-message screen and a message thread with operator alerts and citizen replies
blocks.caption: The annotation that mattered: an emergency button always on screen, not buried in a menu.

sections.heading: Emergency Situation Tracking

blocks.value: During an incident, citizens **check in with their location** and receive alerts from operators. The message list keeps a running record: check-ins, reports, tracking state, and a failed send with a one-tap **Retry**, so a bad connection during an emergency doesn't mean a lost report.

blocks.alt: An AtHoc message list under a "Facility Fire" alert showing check-ins, an emergency report, and a failed report with a Retry button
blocks.caption: A failed report doesn't vanish. It sits in the list with a Retry, not a silent retry loop.

blocks.value: The report itself is a **single composed message**: text, an automatic location pin, and an attached photo, sent as one unit an operator can act on immediately.

blocks.alt: The AtHoc emergency-message composer: a text message, a dropped location pin, and an attached photo of a building fire, ready to send
blocks.caption: One message, three kinds of evidence: text, a location pin, and a photo, sent together.

sections.heading: Interactive Maps

blocks.value: Operators **publish map layers and pins** so first responders and civilians see the same incident: the affected area shaded, new pins flagged, so no one is working from a verbal description of where to go.

blocks.alt: The app map view with a shaded alert zone and two dropped pins marked NEW
blocks.caption: A shaded zone and two flagged pins: everyone sees the same incident, not a description of it.

sections.heading: One System, Every Screen

blocks.value: The mobile app is one face of a larger platform. **Operators work a synchronized tablet and desktop view**, messages and the live map side by side, so field and command stay in step.

blocks.alt: The AtHoc tablet layout with a message list on the left and a full incident map with alert zone and pins on the right
blocks.caption: Same message list, same map, now side by side: the view built for command, not the field.

blocks.value: That consistency didn't happen by accident. I maintained a **shared design-pattern library**, buttons, form fields, menus, alerts, contextual help, used identically across the phone, tablet, and desktop surfaces, so the system read as one product instead of three.

blocks.alt: A UI pattern library sheet: buttons, form fields, dropdowns, popovers, pills, and contextual help styled consistently
blocks.caption: One shared library of buttons, fields, and alerts, not three apps that happen to look similar.

sections.heading: Reflection

blocks.value: The **EMERGENCY button** sits in the top navigation bar on every screen, deliberately impossible to miss. I never got to test whether that was too easy to trigger by accident, a real risk for a control that's exposed at all times rather than tucked behind a confirmation.

The failed-send **Retry** button assumed a person calm enough to notice a failure and tap a button to fix it. I'd want to revisit that assumption directly with people in an actual bad-connection, high-stress moment: an automatic retry with backoff might serve them better than asking for one more deliberate action.

title: Analytics & Big Data
description: On GE's Industrial Internet platform, the Orchestration Editor shipped with a companion Analytics Catalog, while my Data Explorer concept was well received but never prioritized.
blurb: An Orchestration Editor that shipped on GE's Industrial Internet platform, plus a Data Explorer concept leaders liked but never prioritized.
role: Senior Staff UX Interaction Designer, GE Digital
team: Subject-matter experts and stakeholders in collaborative design sessions

hero.alt: The Predix Insight Data Explorer: a multi-series line chart of asset temperatures above a data grid, with layers and chart-type options alongside
hero.caption: Data Explorer concept: layered charts over the raw data grid, before and after an analytic runs.

blocks.value: I interviewed dozens of data scientists and data engineers to understand how they actually worked, and one thing stood out: **data exploration and data cleansing are a critical part of the data-science process**. I conceived **Data Explorer** as the answer, a visualization tool for evaluating data before and after analytic processing. From a searchable, sortable catalog of data and analytic techniques, users then sequence techniques and business logic together in the **Orchestration Editor** and hook the result up to big-data streams and dashboards.

sections.heading: One Visualizer, Before and After the Analytic

blocks.value: The call was where Data Explorer sits: not only at the start, as a cleanup step, but at **both ends of an analytic run**. Going in, users chart layered assets over their raw data grid to inspect what they're about to analyze. Coming out, the same view opens from an orchestration's results (the breadcrumb runs Orchestration Results, then Data Explorer) to check what the analytic produced. The task flow makes the same choice at product scale: **Data Visualizer** appears under Upload and again under Evaluate, marked as a shared component, one visualizer rather than two. Product management and executive leaders responded well to Data Explorer, but it was never prioritized for development.

blocks.alt: An Analytic Cloud task-flow diagram mapping user tasks to Data Explorer, Analytics Catalog, and Analytics Workbench across five columns, from Upload to Evaluate
blocks.caption: One Data Visualizer serves Upload at the start and Evaluate at the end of the five-step flow.

sections.heading: Red Until Configured, Green When Ready

blocks.value: The **Orchestration Editor** shipped, alongside a companion product, the **Analytics Catalog** (the second lane of the task flow above), where users search and filter analytics, read their profiles and ratings, and add them to a library. In the editor, users sequence data, analytics, and business logic on a BPMN-style canvas: standard and long-running analytics, gateways with explicit conditions, sub-processes, and a chart at the end. The interaction I designed puts status on the connection itself. Users drag components from a My Resources drawer onto the canvas and connect them, and a **Connection Editor** opens for the selected analytic, where available fields are dragged onto its inputs. A connection is red while it's improper or incomplete and turns green once it's properly configured, so a broken workflow shows where it's broken.

blocks.alt: The Predix Insight Orchestration Editor: a canvas with data-object, analytic, gateway, and sub-process nodes, and a gateway-conditions panel below
blocks.caption: Analytics, data, and business logic on one BPMN-style canvas, gateway conditions below.

blocks.alt: A six-frame storyboard for the Analytic Application Workbench: a welcome modal, a new-application dialog, components dragged onto a canvas, then connections turning from red to green as fields are dragged onto inputs
blocks.caption: Storyboard: a green arrow means a configured connection, red flags an incomplete one.

blocks.value: The drag-a-field-onto-an-input gesture is in the hand sketches and carries through to the comp, where field tokens fill the gateway conditions. The same page of sketches holds the other end of the workflow: a dashboard, and a dashboard designer for showing multiple outputs.

blocks.alt: Hand sketches of an orchestration editor with a library drawer, a field-to-input drag interaction, a dashboard, and a dashboard designer showing multiple outputs
blocks.caption: In the hand sketches: the field-to-input drag already there, beside a dashboard designer.

sections.heading: A Sticky-Note Wall That Became the Five-Step Task Flow

blocks.value: I ran **collaborative design sessions with subject-matter experts**, sketching wireframes on paper and mapping the whole user journey on a wall of sticky notes. Involving stakeholders in the design process is an excellent way to give UX ownership to everyone. The wall is where the task flow above began: its notes were already grouped into columns for Upload, Pick, Config, Execute, and Evaluate, and the Connection Editor's tasks, like mapping inputs, were on it too.

blocks.alt: Two people at a table sketching on sheets of paper wireframe templates, with sticky notes and markers beside them
blocks.caption: Wireframing on paper with stakeholders at the table, so ownership of the design is shared.

blocks.alt: A wall of sticky notes in columns mapping a data-analysis user journey from sign-in through upload, catalog, workspace, and evaluation
blocks.caption: The whole user journey on one wall of sticky notes, later the task flow's five columns.

sections.heading: Reflection

blocks.value: Color carries the whole configuration state in the Orchestration Editor, red until configured and green when ready, and color alone is a thin signal. The storyboard captions every arrow in words, but nothing in these artifacts shows a second cue on the arrow itself, so the open question is how that state reads for an engineer who can't tell red from green.

Data Explorer's fate is the other open question. Product management and executive leaders liked it, but it was never prioritized for development, so the bet under it, that evaluating data before and after an analytic is the same job, was never tested against real use. The task flow reuses one visualizer at both ends on a read from the interviews, and whether the results end wanted something more specific is still unanswered.
